title: Problem 06
markdown:
### Problem
The positive integer $n$ can be replaced by $ab$, if $a$ and $b$ are positive integers with $a + b = n$. Is it possible starting from 11 to obtain 2011 in a finite sequence of such replacements?

### Solution (adapted from the official solution)
Yes, it can be done in many ways (infinitely many, in fact).

A key observation is that with any $n > 1$, $n = (n - 1) + 1$ can be replaced by $(n - 1) \cdot 1 = n - 1$. So if we obtain any integer larger than 2011, we can step down from there to 2011 in steps of 1.

Thus, one solution is:

$$11 = 6 + 5 \to 30 = 15 + 15 \to 225 = 10 + 215 \to 2150 = 2149 + 1 \to 2149,$$

and repeating the $m = (m-1) + 1 \to m-1$ decrement operation eventually reaches 2011.

### Conceptual Explanation
The partition $n = (n-1) + 1$ allows replacement by $(n-1) \times 1 = n-1$. Hence the operation set includes the predecessor operation $n \to n-1$. By splitting into roughly equal parts, we can quickly grow arbitrarily large: $11 \to 30 \to 225 \to 2150 > 2011$, and then decrement step-by-step to 2011.

### Key Technique
Trivial partition $(n-1) + 1$ generating a step-down decrement operator coupled with multiplicative growth.
